A set is a collection of distinct objects. Basic operations include union, intersection, difference and complement. Set notation is useful for expressing mathematical relationships in economics.
The syllabus includes constant, polynomial, rational, exponential and logarithmic functions. Functions express how one economic variable depends on another.

Linear programming is a method of maximizing or minimizing a linear objective subject to linear constraints. The graphical method is used when the problem can be represented with two decision variables.
Differentiation measures the rate of change of a function. Rules of differentiation are used to obtain derivatives of economic functions.
Maxima and minima help identify the highest or lowest value of a function. In economics they are used in profit maximization and cost minimization.
Partial derivatives measure the change in a multivariable function when one variable changes while the others are held constant.
Differentiation is used to study profit maximization, cost minimization and relationships among total, average and marginal cost and revenue.
Integration is the reverse process of differentiation and is used to obtain totals from marginal functions.
A definite integral measures the accumulated value of a function between specified limits.
Integration is used to calculate consumer surplus, producer surplus, total revenue and total cost from appropriate functions.
A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers. Matrices are useful for representing and solving systems of equations in economic analysis.
The syllabus covers types of matrices, matrix algebra, transpose, inverse and rank.
A determinant is a numerical value associated with a square matrix and is useful in solving systems of linear equations.
Cramer's rule solves a system of linear equations by using determinants, where the required conditions are satisfied.
The matrix inversion method solves a system written in matrix form by multiplying with the inverse of the coefficient matrix when the inverse exists.

Agriculture contributes to food supply, employment, raw materials and rural income and has important linkages with the rest of the economy.
Agriculture supplies food, labour and raw materials to other sectors, while industry and services supply inputs, finance, transport and markets to agriculture.
The farm sector includes cultivation and related activities, while the non-farm sector includes rural manufacturing, trade, transport, construction and services.
Fisheries, horticulture, floriculture and forestry are important allied activities that diversify rural production and income.
Food processing and agro-based industries can create rural employment, add value to agricultural products and strengthen local markets.
Agrarian relations concern social and economic relationships connected with land, cultivation, tenancy, labour and ownership.
Land reforms seek changes in land ownership and use to improve equity and agricultural efficiency. The syllabus studies their evolution from the 1950s onward.
Land utilization describes how land is used, while cropping pattern refers to the distribution of cultivated area among different crops.
Irrigation provides controlled water supply to agriculture and can improve productivity and reduce dependence on rainfall.
Agricultural productivity refers to output obtained from given inputs or land. It varies across regions because of technology, irrigation, infrastructure and other conditions.
Technological change includes improvement in methods, inputs and machinery used in agriculture.
The Green Revolution involved wider use of HYV seeds, fertilizers, irrigation and mechanization, producing major increases in output in selected crops and regions.
Dry land farming uses techniques suited to areas with limited rainfall and seeks efficient conservation of soil moisture.
Biotechnology applies biological knowledge and techniques to agricultural production and crop improvement.

Organic farming emphasizes production methods that avoid or greatly reduce synthetic chemical inputs. Its importance is linked with soil health and sustainability, though it faces production and marketing challenges.
Low productivity can arise from small holdings, inadequate irrigation, weak infrastructure, limited technology, finance and marketing problems.
Agricultural marketing covers movement of farm products from producers to consumers, including storage, transport, grading and sale.
Globalization increases the connection of Indian agriculture with international markets, competition and trade, creating both opportunities and pressures for farmers.

Industrial development contributes to production, employment, technology, productivity and structural transformation of an economy.
Industry is linked with agriculture and services through demand for inputs, supply of machinery, processing, transport, finance and markets.
Industrial classification groups industries according to economic activity and helps organize industrial data and analysis.
Industries may operate in public, private, joint and cooperative sectors. Ownership affects objectives, control and financing.
The private corporate sector consists of companies owned primarily by private shareholders and operating under corporate organization.
MNCs operate in more than one country and can contribute capital, technology and market access, while also raising issues concerning market power and domestic dependence.
Industrial concentration refers to the degree to which production or sales are controlled by a small number of firms. High concentration can create monopoly power.
Industrial location concerns the choice of place for production. Location theories examine factors such as raw materials, markets, labour, transport and costs.
Diversification occurs when an industrial firm expands into new products or activities.
Integration combines stages or activities of production, while merger joins separate business units into a larger organization.
Industrial dispersion means spreading industries across regions rather than concentrating them in a few centres.
Regional imbalance arises when industrial development is unevenly distributed, creating differences in employment, income and infrastructure.
Equity raises funds through ownership claims, while debt finance involves borrowing that must be repaid with agreed interest.
Industrial firms obtain finance from financial institutions and banks for working capital and investment.
Productivity measures output relative to inputs. Higher productivity allows more output from available resources.
Industrial sickness refers to persistent financial and operational weakness that threatens the viability of an industrial unit.
Capacity under-utilization occurs when actual production remains below potential productive capacity. Causes may include weak demand, shortages, finance problems and inefficient management.

The Indian economy is a large mixed developing economy with agriculture, industry and services, considerable regional diversity and continuing problems of poverty, unemployment and inequality.
Demographic features include population size, growth, age and sex composition and other characteristics relevant to economic development.
Over-population refers to a situation where population pressure is high relative to available resources and productive opportunities.
Population policy consists of public measures concerning population growth, health, family welfare and demographic development.
Poverty is serious deprivation of income and resources needed for an acceptable standard of living.
Unemployment occurs when people willing and able to work cannot obtain suitable employment.
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level that reduces the purchasing power of money.
Income inequality refers to unequal distribution of income among individuals or groups.
Economic planning in India was historically organized through Five-Year Plans to guide resource allocation and development priorities.
The 1991 reforms are associated with liberalization, privatization and globalization and marked a major shift in India's economic policy.
NITI Aayog is a policy institution that replaced the Planning Commission and supports policy coordination and development strategy.
The New Industrial Policy reduced several controls and encouraged greater competition and private-sector participation.
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises contribute to production, employment, entrepreneurship and regional development.
Low agricultural productivity is associated with small holdings, irrigation and infrastructure gaps, technology, credit and marketing constraints.
Land reforms seek changes in ownership, tenancy and landholding arrangements to improve equity and productivity.
The Green Revolution increased agricultural output through HYV seeds, irrigation, fertilizers and modern inputs.
Agricultural finance comes from institutional sources such as banks and cooperatives and from non-institutional sources such as informal lenders.
Agricultural marketing includes storage, transport, grading and sale of farm produce and is affected by infrastructure and market access.
Minimum Support Price is a policy price announced for specified crops, while subsidies reduce certain costs or provide support to producers or consumers.
Food security means reliable access to sufficient food. The Public Distribution System distributes specified essential food items through a public network.
The syllabus studies the basic features of Mizoram's agriculture, industry and service sectors.
The regional-economy unit includes sources of revenue, growth of public expenditure and public debt in Mizoram.
Rural development concerns improvement of livelihoods, infrastructure and productive opportunities in Mizoram's rural areas.

Mean is the arithmetic average, median is the middle value in an ordered distribution, and mode is the most frequent value.
Geometric mean is useful for multiplicative changes and growth rates, while harmonic mean is useful for averaging certain rates and ratios.

Skewness measures asymmetry of a distribution, while kurtosis describes its degree of peakedness or flatness.
Probability measures the likelihood of an event. The syllabus covers classical, empirical and modern concepts.
The addition theorem deals with the probability of alternative events, while the multiplication theorem is used for joint occurrence under relevant conditions.
The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with constant success probability.
The Poisson distribution is commonly used for counts of relatively rare events occurring within a fixed interval.
The normal distribution is a continuous, symmetric bell-shaped probability distribution widely used in statistical analysis.
Karl Pearson's coefficient measures the strength and direction of linear association between two variables.
Rank correlation measures association using the ranks of observations rather than their raw numerical values.
Partial correlation studies association between two variables while controlling another, while multiple correlation considers association involving more than two variables.
Regression estimates the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more explanatory variables.
Ordinary Least Squares estimates a regression line by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.
The coefficient of determination indicates the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the regression model.
A time series is a set of observations arranged over time. Its components include trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular movements.
Index numbers measure relative changes in variables such as prices or quantities over time.

International trade is exchange of goods and services across national borders. It allows countries to specialize and obtain goods not produced efficiently at home.
International trade differs from internal trade because it crosses national boundaries and is affected by exchange rates, trade policy and greater differences in laws and factor mobility.
The absolute-advantage approach explains trade through differences in countries' productive efficiency.
Comparative advantage explains gains from specialization according to relative opportunity costs, even when one country is more efficient in producing all goods.
Terms of trade describe the rate at which a country's exports exchange for imports.
Free trade means international exchange with minimal trade restrictions.
Protection uses tariffs, quotas and other measures to restrict imports or support domestic producers.
A tariff is a tax imposed on imported or exported goods, commonly used to raise revenue or protect domestic industry.
A quota directly limits the quantity or value of a good that may be imported.
Balance of trade is the difference between the value of merchandise exports and imports.
Balance of payments is the systematic record of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world during a period.
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another.
Devaluation is an official reduction in a currency's value under a managed or fixed system, while depreciation is a market-driven fall in value.
The World Trade Organization provides a framework of rules and negotiations for international trade among member countries.

Demography is the systematic study of human population, including size, composition, distribution and change.
A census is an official enumeration of the population and provides important demographic and socio-economic data.
Fertility refers to actual childbearing in a population and is measured through demographic rates.
Mortality refers to deaths in a population and is studied through measures such as death rates and life expectancy.
Migration is movement of people from one place to another and changes the size and composition of populations in both origin and destination areas.
Population growth results from the combined effects of births, deaths and migration.
Age and sex composition describe the distribution of population by age groups and sex and influence labour supply and social needs.
Population size and structure affect labour, savings, public services and resource use, while economic development influences fertility, mortality and migration.

The history of economic thought studies the development of economic ideas and theories over time and the historical conditions in which they emerged.
Classical economists emphasized production, markets, distribution and long-run economic development.
Adam Smith emphasized division of labour, markets and the role of self-interest within a system of exchange.
Ricardo made major contributions to theories of value, distribution, rent and comparative advantage.
Malthus is associated with population theory and arguments concerning population growth and resources.
Marx analysed capitalism through class relations, production, accumulation and conflict.
Marginalist analysis shifted attention toward marginal utility, marginal productivity and individual choice.
Keynes transformed macroeconomic thought by emphasizing aggregate demand, unemployment and the possibility of equilibrium below full employment.
